title: A Single Voice in an Imperfect World
body:
Dear friend,

As autumn deepens in Japan, Jōdo Shū temples hold an observance called Jūya, meaning “Ten Nights.” Long ago, people gathered over ten days and ten nights to recite the name of Amida Buddha: Namu Amida Butsu.

The teaching behind this observance tells us that doing good for ten days and nights in this troubled world is more precious than doing good for a thousand years in a land where nothing stands in the way.

This is not because our world is peaceful or easy. It is because it is not.

We live with worry. We are hurried by our work and responsibilities. At times, even when we know better, we say words that hurt someone or make choices we later regret. Before we notice it, we may have gone many days without giving our own hearts a moment of rest.

Perhaps this is why a single recitation of Namu Amida Butsu matters so much.

We often think, “I will pray when my mind is calm.” Or, “I will turn toward the Buddha when I have become a better person.” But if we wait until our minds are perfectly settled, that day may never come.

The nembutsu is not a practice reserved for people who have already become complete. It is a way home for those of us who are still finding our way. It can be spoken on a busy morning, in the quiet of a tired night, or in the middle of a day filled with regret.

To say Namu Amida Butsu once is not to make every problem disappear. It is to remember that we do not have to carry our imperfect lives alone. It is to turn, even briefly, toward the compassion that has never turned away from us.

If you can find a small pause today, try saying these words softly, aloud or in your heart: Namu Amida Butsu. You do not need to prepare yourself first. You do not need to become someone else.

Just as you are, you may return.
